LESSON: INTERACTIVE SPEAKING

Grade: Grade 9
Subject: ARABIC
Strand: Listening and Speaking
Topic 1.9: Interactive Speaking

SECTION 1: WELCOME

Hello! This is a study lesson on Interactive Speaking. Read the explanation, follow every worked example, then do the practice. This is original CBC Learn content written from KICD outcomes — not a copy of a commercial textbook.

Big question: Why should we use polite language when interacting with others?

SECTION 2: WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. identify basic greetings in formal contexts
2. apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication
3. appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication

SECTION 3: STUDY NOTES (READ AND LEARN)

WHAT YOU ARE STUDYING: INTERACTIVE SPEAKING
Subject: ARABIC · Grade: Grade 9
This is a learner study lesson (not a teacher guide). Read every part, follow the models, then practise.

BIG PICTURE
Interactive Speaking helps you succeed in ARABIC. You will understand it, practise it, and use it at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

KEY FACTS: INTERACTIVE SPEAKING
Language skills grow by daily practice: listen carefully, speak clearly, read every day, write neatly.
Model → guided practice → independent practice.
Always use complete sentences when writing answers.

PART 1: Identify basic greetings in formal contexts

What this means
In this part you learn to identify basic greetings in formal contexts. You will use ideas from at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: identify basic greetings in formal contexts.
2. Listen, speak, read, then write using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Model reading: Read a short paragraph about “Interactive Speaking”, then retell it in 3 sentences.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can identify basic greetings in formal contexts. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 2: Apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication

What this means
In this part you learn to apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication. You will use ideas from at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication.
2. Listen, speak, read, then write using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Model speaking: Say 4 clear sentences about Interactive Speaking to a partner.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 3: Appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication

What this means
In this part you learn to appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication. You will use ideas from at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication.
2. Listen, speak, read, then write using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Model writing: Write 5 neat sentences using new words from this lesson.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication. Write or say your answer clearly.

PUT IT TOGETHER
Close your notes and say aloud: what Interactive Speaking is, one example, and one way you will practise this week.

SECTION 4: QUICK EXAMPLES

Example 1: Read a short paragraph about “Interactive Speaking”, then retell it in 3 sentences. (skill: identify basic greetings in formal contexts)

Example 2: Say 4 clear sentences about Interactive Speaking to a partner. (skill: apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication)

Example 3: Write 5 neat sentences using new words from this lesson. (skill: appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication)

SECTION 5: PRACTICE NOW

1. Write 5 sentences (or show 5 clear steps) that teach Interactive Speaking to a classmate.
2. Practise this skill: identify basic greetings in formal contexts.
3. Practise this skill: apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication.
4. Practise this skill: appreciate the need for active listening for effective communication.
5. Make one local Kenya example of Interactive Speaking from your county, market, farm, or school.
6. Mark your own work: What did you get right? What will you redo?

SECTION 6: WORK TO DO (HOME / REVISION)

1. In your exercise book, make a one-page revision sheet for Interactive Speaking: meaning, 3 examples, 5 practice items.
2. Teach a parent/guardian or younger sibling one part of this lesson (2 minutes).
3. Answer in writing: Why should a Grade 9 learner study Interactive Speaking?
4. Prepare for the quiz: cover the Remember box and recite it.

SECTION: THINK ABOUT IT

1. Why should we use polite language when interacting with others?

SECTION: REMEMBER

1. Know what Interactive Speaking means in your own words.
2. Use local Kenyan examples, not only definitions.
3. Practise in small steps, then check your work.
4. Be able to: identify basic greetings in formal contexts.
5. Be able to: apply non-verbal cues that show active listening for effective communication.

Now complete the Revision Quiz. Open Answers only after you finish.

— CBC Learn · Original study notes from KICD outcomes (Strategy 2)
